titleStmt.title: An interim TEI edition of Nehemiah Wharton's letters

availability.p: The original letters were created in 1642, and the text was first published in 1853.
The original text is out of copyright in the UK because it was first published more than 50 years ago, and the author must have died more than 70 years ago.
The original text is out of copyright in the US because it was first published before 1923.
There is no new copyright in this transcript because it is an unoriginal copy of an existing work.
If any new intellectual property rights have arisen in XML markup or editorial additions, these rights are waived under CC0.

sourceDesc.p: These manuscripts are letters sent from Nehemiah Wharton to George Willingham from August to October 1642. Internal evidence shows that Willingham was a London merchant, and that Wharton had been his servant and at the time of writing was a sergeant in the infantry regiment of Denzil Holles in the parliamentary army commanded by the Earl of Essex. The letters describe the activities of this regiment during the early months of the First Civil War.

The letters are preserved among the State Papers in the UK National Archives. It is not certain how these private letters came to be part of this collection. The letters were first published by Sir Henry Ellis in 1853 but with many transcription errors. A more accurate transcript but with added punctuation was published in Calendar of State Papers Domestic in 1887.

correction.p: Text was manually transcribed from digital photos of microfilm. OCR errors are not expected. Keying errors are possible but are likely to be minimal because many quality checks have been carried out.
Original spelling has been retained throughout.
Where obvious errors in the original text can be corrected, choice tags with matching pairs of sic and corr tags have been used.

normalization.p: Abbreviations are marked up with choice tags containing matching pairs of abbr and expan tags, which in turn can contain am and ex tags where appropriate.
Deletions and insertions are both included and have been marked up with del and add tags.
The following characters are represented by choice tags containing matching pairs of orig and reg tags: i/j and u/v used interchangeably; ff representing F at the start of a word; long s.
Superscript is represented by @rend="sup" in am, add, and seg tags.
Subscript is represented by @rend="sub" in add tags.
Highlighting indicated in the original text by underlining or a box around text is represented by hi. Manicules are not represented.

quotation.p: No quotation marks are present in the source text.

hyphenation.p: No hyphens are present in the source text.

namespace.tagUsage: Contains 9 text elements containing the original letters.
The outer text element is a composite text consisting of all of Wharton's original letters. Each of the text elements contained within the group represents one letter: @n is TNA document reference.
Contains all of each letter. Letters have no front or back matter.
Original letters mostly consist of a single paragraph but smaller paragraphs may be used in postscript or in address div1.

Inside body of letters, the first is the main text of the letter, including opener and closer, the second is the address written on the outside of the letter. This address appears on the final folio as the manuscript is now arranged.
Contains any dateline and salute at start of letter.
Contains any salute and signature at end of letter.
Used for any addition to letter after closer, but not for address on final folio, which uses div1.
Page breaks in original manuscript. @n is folio number. These tags should not have any whitespace either side of them in the source code. Any whitespace needed should be added by XSL.

Line breaks in original manuscript. These tags should not have any whitespace either side of them in the source code. This is to make it easier to preserve original line breaks in HTML and Markdown. Any whitespace needed should be added by XSL. Line breaks are taken to be implied and so not explicitly represented at start of contents of these tags: opener, p, closer, signed, salute, dateline; or immediately after these milestone tags: pb.
Used to group matching pairs of tags representing features according to alternative transcription conventions: sic, corr; orig, reg; abbr, expan; orig containing gap, supplied.

Illegible or missing text. Reason specified in @reason. This is usually because of damage to the original manuscript, or illegible deletions. If the missing text can be inferred, gap is nested in orig then in choice, and paired with supplied.
Text missing from a gap that can be inferred. Should be nested in a choice tag with a matching orig tag containing a gap tag.
Text is present and can be read but reading is uncertain.
Words that contain expanded abbreviations. Should be paired with matching abbr tag inside choice.
Part of word that was abbreviated.
Abbreviated form of word used in original text. Should be paired with matching expan tag inside choice.
Abbreviation mark in abbreviated word in original text. @rend="sup" indicates that this is otherwise a normal letter but rendered as superscript. Also used for ampersand without @rend.

Highlighted text. Where @rend is "outline" this means a line drawn around outside of block. Most of these passages relate to the lieutenant-colonel. The highlighting was probably added later by someone other than Wharton. Where @rend is "underlined" this means the text is underlined. It is not clear whether this was done by Wharton or a later reader. Manicules are not currently represented.
Text inserted in original manuscript. @rend records whether it is superscript or subscript.
Text deleted by the author but still readable. Usually struck through. Illegible deletions use gap.

Used to indicate errors that occur in the original manuscript. These are mostly repeated words and words that appear to have missing letters. Identification of errors is based on Wharton's usage elsewhere in the text, particularly where he has made a correction by inserting a missing letter as superscript; unnecessary repeated words; and missing letters that make a word phonetically different. Should be nested in a choice tag with a matching corr tag.

Corrected version of text that has been judged erroneous and marked up with sic. Should be nested in a choice tag with a matching sic tag. Contents of this tag do not represent original letter forms such interchangeable i/j or u/v, long s, or ff for F, because it is only intended to be used in clean versions where reg would be used instead of orig. Otherwise it follows Wharton's spelling as closely as possible.
Contains date and place of each letter. Usually given at the start but sometimes at the end. Dates are then marked up with date tags and place names with rs.
Dates given anywhere in the text. @when-custom is in standard form yyyy-mm-dd. All dates are in the Julian calendar and have not been modernized. @when is not used.
Formal salutes at beginning and end of letters. Person being saluted marked up with rs.
Signature at end of letters. Usually Wharton's full name but sometimes initials. Name also marked up with rs.
Marks change to a hand other than Wharton's.

Used to mark up all names and some other strings that refer to named entities. Classes of named entities represented are: people, animals, places, organizations, events, but these are not yet classified by @type. Texts, such as references to specific letters, are not classed as named entities. Strings referring to people are marked up if they contain any individual information, even if the person cannot be identified in practice. Generic descriptors such as "soldier" or "maid" are not marked up. The King is only marked up where the string refers to the King's person, not when it is used to signify allegiance. Similarly, Parliament is only marked up when it refers to actions by Parliament or membership of either house, not when it is used to signify allegiance. Pronouns are not marked up as referring directly to an entity, but are sometimes incidentally marked up as part of a string that refers to a related entity, such as "his house" or "my mistress". Fictional entities such as God, Sodom, and Gomorrah are not marked up. Sir Guy is treated as a fictional entity and not marked up, but his cave is marked up as a real place. Algiers and Malta are not marked up because they are used to refer more to stereotypes or ideas than to real locations. Strings such as "the city" are not marked up if they refer to the inhabitants more than the place.

Used for two different purposes. Where @type="entry": splits the main paragraph of each letter into shorter sections for ease of reading and more precise representation of the logical structure of the text. The main text of each letter consists of one very long paragraph but within this paragraph it is written in the style of a diary, with an entry for each day's events. These entries are not set off as paragraphs in the original manuscript but can be interpreted as logical divisions of the text. Not used for paragraphs which are all about the same topic, which usually includes postscripts and the address on the back of each letter. Where @type="ordinal": indicates ordinal numbers, usually with @rend="sup" to indicate superscript. This has no semantic meaning and is only used to reproduce the visual appearance of the manuscript in semi-diplomatic renditions of the text.

Indicates original characters where i/j or u/v have been used interchangeably, or ff has been used for F, or where a long s has been used. These should be children of a choice tag with a matching reg tag containing the modernized version. Also wrapped around gap tags where missing text that can be inferred needs a matching supplied tag. This is why number of occurrences does not match reg.

Indicates modernized characters where i/j or u/v have been used interchangeably, or ff has been used for F, or where a long s has been used. These should be children of a choice tag with a matching orig tag containing the original version.

calendar.p: The Julian calendar as used in 17th-century England. The start date of the year is unspecified because the texts in this file do not contain any dates between 1 January and 25 March.

p.seg:
on Munday August the 8th we marched to Acton but beinge
the 6th company we were belated and many of our ſsoildiers were constrained
to lodge in beds whoſse feathers were abouve a yard longe

Tueſsday early
in the morninge ſseuverall of our ſsoildiers inhabitinge the out parts
of the towne ſsallied out vunto the houſse of one Penrudduck a
papist and beinge baſsely affronted by him and his dogge entred his
houſse and pilladged him to the purpoſse this day alſso the ſsoildiers
got into the Church defaced the auntient and ſsacred glaſsed picturs
and Burned the holy railes

Wenſsday MrMaster Louve gauve vus a famous
ſsermon this day also the ſsoildiers brought the holy railes from
Chiſſssick and burned them in our towne at chiſſssick they also intended
to pillage the Lord of Portlands houſse and alſso Doctor Ducke
but by our Commanders they were preuvented This day our genell ſsoldiers
generally manifested their diſslike of our Leiftenant Colonell
who is a Godamme blade and doubtleſſsse hatch in Hell and wee
all deſsire that ether the Parlaiment would depoſse him or God
conuvert him or the Divill fetch him a way quick This day
Towards euven our Regiment marched to VUxbridge but I was
left behind to bringe vup 30 men with ammunition the next morning

Thurſsday I marched towards VUxbridge and at Hillington one mile
from VUxbridge the railes beinge gone wee got the ſsurplaſſsse to
make vus handcherchers and one of our ſsoildiers ware it to vuxbridge
this day the Railes of VUxbridge formerly remouved was with the
ſseruvice boock burned this euven MrMaster Hardinge gauve vus a werthy
ſsermon

ffFryday I with 3 other commaunders were ſsent with
100 Muſsqetteres to bringe the ammunition to Amerſsam in
Buckinham shire which is the ſsweetest Country that euver
I ſsaw and as is the cuntrey ſso also is the people but
wantinge roome for the Regiment comminge after vus we were
constrained to march 4 miles further vunto greate Miſſssenden
where we had noble entertainment from the whole towne but
espetially from SrSir Brian Ireſson and the minister of the towne

Satturday morninge our companies overtoke vus and we marched
together vunto Alſsberry and after we had marched a longe mile
ffFor ſso they are all in this Cuntrey vuntill wee came to Wendeuver
where wee looted refreſſsshed ourſseluves burnt the railes and accidentally
one of Captaine ffFrancis his men forgettinge he was charged with a
bullet ſshot a maide through the head and ſshe immediately died
from hence wee marched very ſsadly 2 miles wher Colonell
Hamden accompanied with many Gentlemen well horſsed met vus
and with greate IJoy ſsaluted and welcomed vus and conducted vus
vunto Alſsbury where we hauve a Regiment of foote and seuverall
Troopes of horſse to ijoyne with vus in this towne our welcome
is ſsuch that wee want nothinge but a good Leiftenant Colonell

Sabath day August the 1514 in this towne a pulpit was built in the
market place where wee heard 2 worthy ſsermons this euveninge
our vungodley Leiftenant Colonel vupon an vungrounded whimsey commaunded
2 of our Captaines namely Captaine ffFrancis and Captaine Beacon
with their companies to march out of the towne but they went
not euvery day our ſsoildiers by stealth doe visit papists houſses
and constraine from them both meate and money they giuve them
whole greate louves and Cheſſsses which they triumphantly carry
away vupon the points of their ſswords

seg.hi:
I humbly intreate you
as you deſsire the ſsucceſſsse of our IJust and honorable cause
that you would indeauvor to Roote out our Leiftenant Colonell
for if wee march further vunder his commaund we feare vupon
ſsuffitient grounds wee are all but dead men

p.seg:
Munday August the 1615th
Colonell Hamden marched out of Aliſsbury with 400 muſsquetters
and about an hundred Horſse towards wattleton in Oxfordſshire
where the Commiſſssion of aray was this day to be ſsetled but they
hearinge of the aproch of our troopes fled and our horſse
pſsuedperſsued them ſso cloſse that SrSir John Curſsam was taken and
the lord of Barkes was Constrained to take Aſsgate houſs ſsometime
the Lord of Carnarvans where our companies hauve at this
preſsent beſset him and thus much for the preſsent:

touchinge
Leiftenant Colonell Biddeman formentioned I once more humbly
beseech you and not I alone but many others both commaunders
officers and common ſsoildiers that you would indeuvor to Rout him
There are ſseuveral other circumstances which I want time to
expreſſsse for the office aſſssigned mee is very troublesome and
Continually takes vup my whole time and therfore for the
preſsent let these ſsatiſsfie. to conclude I preſsent you
and miſstris with my humble ſseruvice and doe giuve you humble
and harty thankes for all your former and late fauvors and
doe intreate you to remember my humble ſseruvice to MrMaster Molloyne
and wife my ſseruvice also to Elizabeth Anna John and ſsammuell
which I often thinke vupon. and alſso my louve to all my fellow
ſseruvants In extreame hast I rest

closer.salute:
Your poore auntient humble and
affectionate ſseruvant to commaund

To the worthy and his
much Honored ffFrend
MrMaster George Willingham merchant
at the golden

Lane

p.seg:
august the 17 our companies after they had taken ſsixe
delinquents and ſsent them to London returned to Aliſsbury this day
wee receiuved 6 feild peeces and 2 troopes of horse with other neſſsseſſssaries for warre

wenſsday morninge
a warwick ſshire minister which the Caluvalleres had pillaged to the
ſskin gauve vus a ſsermon after noone our regiment marchd in to the
feild and ſskirmished

Thurſsday morninge another ſsermon was
giuven us after noone our 4 regiment marched in to the feild but by
reson of foule weather were immediatly diſsmiſſssed this night our
regiment were commaunded to march the next morninge by 4 of the
clock vunder our leiftenant Colonell but our ſsargeants resoluved
to ſsurrender their halberts and the ſsoildiers their armes and not
to march

ffFryday very early in the morninge our leiftenant
Colonell was Caſshered for which I giuve you harty thankes and
ſsargeant Maijor Quarles imployed in his roome wherat both
commaunders officers and ſsoildiers excedingly reijoyſsed this morninge
wee cherfully marched towards Buckingham in the reare of
Colonell Chomleys regiment by reaſson wherof wee could get
no quarter there but were constrained to quarter our ſseluves about
the cuntrey whervupon I and 3 gentlemen of my company
viſsited that thrice noble gentleman SrSir Richard Ingliſsby
where his owne table was our quarter and Sargeant Maijor
Barrif and his ſsonne captaine Ingliſsby and ſseuverall other noble
gentlemen were our comrades

ſsaturday early in the morninge
I departed hence and gathered a compleate file of my owne men
about the cuntrey and marched to SrSir Alexander Dentons his
parke who is a malignant fellow and killed a fat buck fastened
his head vupon my Halbert and commanded 2 of my pickes
to bringe the body after mee to Buckingham with a guard
of muſsqetteeres comminge theither with part of it I feasted
my Captaine captaine Parcker Captaine Beacon and Colonell
Hamdens ſsonne and with the rest ſseuverall Leiftenants
Enſseignes and ſsargeants and had much thankes for my pains this
day our ſsargeant Maijor Generall came vunto vus and declared the
commaund giuven him ouver our Regiments

Sunday morninge wee
marched from Buckingham in to northampton ſshire a longe and
tedious ijorney wantinge both bread and water and about 10 at
night came vunto Byfeild in diſspight of our enemies at which
Towne we could get no quarter neither meate drinke nor
lodginge and had we not bin ſsuplyed with 10 cart loade of
prouviſsion and beare from Banbury many of vus had periſshed
this night our company was commaunded to guard the towne all
night which after a longe and tedious march vunto mee was
very greuvious

MudayMunday morninge wee marched in to
Warwick ſshire with about 3000 foote and 400 horſse
vuntill we came to Southum in the way we tooke 2 Caluvaller
Spies this is a very malignant towne both miniſster adand people
we pillaged the minister and tooke from him a drum and ſseuveral
armes this night our ſsoildiers wearied out quartered themſseluves
about the towne for foode and lodginge but before we could
eate or drinke an alarum cryed arme arme for the enemy
is comminge and in halfe an hour all our ſsoildiers though diſsperſsd were compleate
in armes ready to encounter the enemy cryinge out for a diſsh of
caluvalleres to ſsupper our horſse were quartered about the cuntrey
but the enemy came not whervupon our ſsoildiers cryed out to hauve a
breakefast of Cauvallers. we strongly barecadoed the towne and
at euvery paſſssage placed our ordinance and watched it all night
our ſsoildiers contented to lye vupon hard stones

in the morninge
early our enemies conſsiſstinge of about eight hundred horſse
and three hundred foote horse with ordinance led by the Earle of
north hampton the lord of Carnaruvan and the Lord Compton &and
captaine Legge and others intended to ſset vupon vus before wee could
gather our companies together but beinge ready all night early
in the morninge wee went to meete them with a few troopes of
horſse and ſsixe feild peeces and beinge on fier to meete be at
them wee marched thorow the corne and got the hill
of them whervupon thethey played vupon vus with ther ordinances but
they came ſshort our gunner tooke ther owne bullet ſsent it to them
againe and killed 2 horſse and 2 men after we gauve them
eight ſshot more whervupon all their foote companies fled
and offered ther armes in the townes adijacent for tweluve
pence a peece ther p troopes whelinge about toke vup ther
Tooke vup their dead bodies and fled but the horſse they
left behind them ſsome of them hauvinge ther guts beaten
out on both ſsides the number of men ſslaine as themſseluvs report
was fifty beſsides horſse. one drummer beinge dead at the
bottom of the hill our Knapſsack boyes rifled to the ſshirt
which was very lowzy an other drummer we fownd 2 miles
of with the his armes ſshot of and lay a diinge ſseuveral dead
corps wee found in corne feilds and amongst them a trumpeter
whose trumpet our horſsmen ſsounded into Couventry wee toke ſseuveral
priſsoners and amongst them Captaine Legge and captaine
Clarke from thence we marched valiantly after them toward
Couventry and at dunſsmore heath they threatned to
giuve vus battaile but we got the hill of them ordered our
men and cryed for a messe of Caluvalleres to ſsupper as wee
had to breake fast but they all fled and we immediately
marched vunto Couventry where the Countrey met vus and
in armes and welcommed vus and gauve vus good quarter
both for horſse and foote in this battell I met with your
horſseman Dauvy and he and I preſsent you and my Miſstris
with our most humble ſseruvice deſsiringe you to pray for vus
and doubt not but both of will valiantly fight the Lords
battaile thus with my seruvice to MrsMistress Eelizabeth Anna
John and Samuell and my louve to all my fellow ſseruvants
I rest

postscript.p:
I pray preſsent the humble ſseruvice of Gregory Kent and my ſselfe vunto MrMaster
Molloyne with my best reſspects to MrMaster Henry Hickman and
informe him that I hauve receiuved his booke and ſshall acknowledge
my ſselfe ingaged for the ſsame I would hauve written vunto him and
others my kindred and frends but I want time and therfore
must humbly in treate you to informe them therof I earnestly
deſsire to heare from you whether you receiuved a letter dated August the
17th or not

div1.p:
To his much honored frend
MrMaster George Willingham
marchant at the
golden Anchor in
StSaint Swethins Lane

p.seg:
as time pmitspermits I deſsire to acquaint you with the paſſssages
of my pilgramage my last vunto you was from Couventry August the 26th
which place is still our quarter a City inuvironed with a wall coequall if not
excedinge that of London for breadth and height the compaſse of it
is neare 3 miles all of free stone it hath 4 stronge gates stronge
battlements stored with towers bulwarkes courts of guard and other
neſſsseſſssaries this City hath magnificent churches and stately streetes
with in it ther are also ſseuverall ſsweete and plaſsantpleasant ſspringes of water
built of freestone very large ſsuffitient to supply many thousand men
this City gates are guarded day and night with 400 armed men
and no man entreth in or out but opon examination Thursday
it is also very ſsweetly Cituate

Thurſsday august the 26th our
ſsoildiers pillaged a malignant fellowes houſse in this City
and the Lord brooke immediately proclaimed that whoſsoeuver
ſshould for the future offend in that kind ſshould hauve Martiall
law this day commaund that was giuven that all ſsoildiers
ſshould attend their colors every morne by ſsixe of the clock
to march into the feild to practiſse which is done accordingly

ffFryday ſseuverall of our ſsoildiers both horſse and foote ſsallyed
out of the City vunto the Lord Dunſsmores parke and brought
from thence greate store of Veniſson which is as good
as euver I tasted and I euver ſsince they make it their
dayly practiſse ſso that veniſson is almost as common
with vus as beefe with you this day our horſsemen ſsallyed
out as their dayly custome is and brought in with them two
Cauvaleeres and with them an old baſse preist the parſson
of Sowe neare vus and led him rediculouſsly about the
City vunto the cheife Commaunders this day I againe meet
with Dauvy your horſseman and both horse and man are in good caſse

Saturday I met with your auntient maide ſseruvant
Lydea with her father and her brethren who all wept
for ijoy when they ſsaw mee an officer in this Deſseigne
for the day wee marched into Couventry the Rebels had
command to pillage Anstey the habitation of her
father and Bromagam the place of her and her
husbands dwellinge both which are but 3 miles
from Couventry ſshe hath bin maried 3 yeares
and preſsents her ſseruvice vunto you and my mistris and your children
her father inuvited mee and 20 of the cheife of my company
to dinner at Anstey but time would not ſsuffer vus to
accept it This day a whore which had followed our
Campe from London was taken by the ſsoildiers and
first led about the City then ſset in the pillory after
in the cage then duckt in a riuver and at the last
baniſsht the City

Sunday morne the Lord of Eſſsseyx
his Chaplaine MrMaster Kemme the Coopers ſsonne preched
vunto vus and this was the first sermon we heard
ſsince wee came from Alisbury but before he had ended
his first prayer newes was brought in to the Church
unto our Commaunders that Noneaton ſsome ſsixe miles
from vus was fired by the enemy and forthwith our
Generall and ſseuverall Captaine iſſssued forth but I and
many others stayed vuntill ſsermon was ended after
which wee were commaunded to march forth with
all ſspeede namely my Captaine with Captaine Beacon
and Captaine ffFrancis of our regiment and of other
regiments in all to the number of 1000 foote and one troope
of horſse but before wee came at them they ran all
away not hauvinge done much harme whervupon wee
returned to Couventry againe with a commaund to
be ready in armes by fiuve in the morninge next
vupon paine of death our men are very corragious
and that they may ſso continue wee deſsire accordinge
to promiſse a ſsupply of faithfull able miniſsters which
wee excedingly want this morninge wee are
marchinge forth to pſsueperſsue the rebels and that we may
obtaine victory we againe deſsire your earnest and
constant prayers Thus with my humble ſseruvice to
your ſselfe and my Mistris and alſso vunto all
Your Children and alſso my louve to all my fellow
ſseruvants whether with you or from you for the preſsent
in extreame hast I rest but not to remaine
till death

closer.salute:
Your humble Louvinge and
thanckfull ſseruvant

postscript.p:
I pray preſsent my most humble ſseruvice
vunto MrMaster Molloyne &and MrMaster William Willingham &and
my Aunt MrMaster Hawkins MrMaster Rudduck
MrMaster Kinſsman MrMaster Watſson and the rest
of my louvinge frends and acquaintance

I humbyhumbly intreate you fauvorably to accept theſse rude
lines for I want time either to write or compoſse
them in a more comely forme I earneſstly
deſsire to heare of the occurrences of London

p.seg:
Munday august the 29 before we had marched 2 miles
towards the Cauvalleeres wee were informed by the post that 60 of
them weere taken and impriſsoned in northhampton and the rest fled
whervupon wee returned vunto Couventry and our company were immediately
commaunded to guard part of the City and a gate called Newgate about
midnight our ſsoildiers on the wall diſscouvered fier in the City neare
StSaint mary hall our magazene which accidentally began at a bakery
houſse and in 3 or 4 howers was quenched and no greate harme done
but the Citizens were much affrighted

Tueſsday morninge we officers
weet our halberts with a barrell of stronge beare called ould
hum which wee gauve our ſsoildiers this day MrMaster Jephcot feasted
mee and ſseuverall of my Company in Couventry this euven our ſsoildiers
brought a cart loade of armes from SrSir Robert ffFiſshers ſsome 6 miles
from Couventry with his owne picture standinge very stately in the cart

wenſsday wee kept the fast and heard 2 ſsermons but before the
third was ended wee had an alaram to march preſsently by ten
of the clock wee got our regiments together and kept our
randevow in the City vuntill midnight and about two in the morninge
marched out of this City towards Northampton this City hath
4 steeples 3 Churches 2 pariſshes and not longe ſsince but one
preist but now the world is well amended with them this morne
I was exceedinge ſsick and the pallet of my mouth fell downe but
Captaine beacon to my louvinge frend I vupon our march sent a mile
for a little pepper and put it vup againe This day our ſsouldiers brought
with them 3 aſſsses which they had taken out of the Lord Dunſsmores
Parke which they loaded with their Knapſsackes and dignified them
with the name of the Lord Dunſsmore

this day beinge Thurſsday
wee marched ouver dunſsmore heath neare 12 miles without any
ſsustenance inſsomuch that many of our ſsoildiers dranke stinkinge
water vuntill wee came vunto Barby in North Hampton Shire where
the cuntrey accordinge to their ability releived us as many of vus as
they could our ſsoildiers pillaged the parſson of this towne and brought
him away priſsoner with his ſsurplaſſsse and other relicks from hence
wee marched 4 miles further vunto Longe Bugby where we had
very hard quarter in ſsomuch that many of our Captaines could
get no lodginge and our ſsoildiers were glad to diſspoſſsseſse the very
ſswine and as many as could quartered in the Church but here
your man Dauvy ridinge before our foote companies got mee
both foode and lodginge this towne hath for 2 ſsundayes together
bin so abused by the rebels that both men women and children were
glad to leauve the towne and hide themſseluves in ditches and
corne feilds

Fryday early in the morninge fryday morninge early
a meſſssenger came to our Colonell that in the Kinges houſse called
Homby 3 miles distant there were 500 muſsketters to cut of all our
Our straglinge ſsoildiers wherby wee preuvented them this morninge
our soildiers ſsallyed out about the cuntrey and returned in state clothed
with a ſsurplaſſsse hoode and cap representinge the Biſshop of Canterbury
from hence wee marched 2 miles wher Homby houſse stands very
stately vupon a hill and the Lord of Northhamptons house and parke
neare vunto it but we could not restraine our ſsoildiers from
entringe his his parke and killinge his Deare and had not the lord
Gray and our ſsargent major Generall withstod them they had pillagd
his house this euven we marched vunto North hampton where the
towneſsmen hearinge of our cominge marched marched out into the Cuntrey
to preuvent the commission of aray intended to be ſsetled by the Lord
Mountagu and others which Mountagu they brought priſsoner
vunto north hampton and preuvented his deſseigne this euveninge
7 troopes of horſse came vunto vus this night the Lord of north
Hampton by stealth came into the towne veiued our horſse forces and
in the morninge diſscouvered but immediately di eſscaped

Saturday
morninge the Lord munijoy and his ſsonne were taken ridinge
through the towne this euveninge all the Sargeants of our Regiment
met together and out of 23 choſse 2 for stewards for a ſsupper
and other more weighty affaires and choſse mee for one of them
which place is exceedinge troubleſsome vunto mee this day came
SrSir arthur Haſsleriges and other troopes into our towne this day our
ſsoildiers brought in much veniſson and other pillage from the
malignants about the Cuntrey this euveninge we feasted all our
Sergeants with ſsome other ſsuperior officers which is very
troubleſsome and chargable and I cannot avoide this night I
inuvited your man Dauvy and his Comrade and made them welcome
Thus with my hublehumble ſseruvice to you my miſstismistris and your ChildreChildren
and my louve to all my fellow ſseuvatsservants in extreme hast I rest

postscript.p: I pray let me heare from you by this berer

div1.p:
To his much Honored ffFrend
MrMaster George Willingham
Marchant at the golden
Anchor in StSaint ſsweethins
Lane giuve these

p.seg:
I preſsent you and my MrsMistress with my humble ſseuviceservice
wiſshinge you and all yours the constant fruition of all hapineſſsse
this is my fifth letter vunto you but I question wheither
euver you receiuved one of them becauſse you neiuver yet honored
mee with a peece of paper I have therfore once more ſsent vunto
you by this bearer Leiftenant Wade who hath promiſsed to
deliuver theſse with his owne hands

our place of randeuvoues
is still at North hampton which for Cituation circuit
and statelyneſse of buildinge exceeds couventry but the walls
are miſserably ruined though the cuntrey abounds in mindes
of stone from hence I hauve nothinge remarkeable to preſsent
you with neither will time permit me to acquaint you with
circumstances

this morninge our regiments beinge drawne
unto the feild to exerciſse many of them diſscouvered their
baſse ends in vundertakinge this deſseigne and demaunded fiuve
ſshillinge a man which they ſsay was promiſsed them monthly
by the comitte or they would ſsurrender their armes
whervupon Colonell hamden and other commaunders labored
to appeaſse them but could not ſso that if they hauve not
the forenamed ſsupply we feare a very greate fraction
amongst vus there is alſso greate deſsention betweene our Troopers
and foote companies for the foote men are much abuſsed and ſsouldiers
pillaged and wounded I my ſselfe hauve lately experimentally found
it for they toke from mee abouve the worth of three pounds
but I am not diſscorged by any of theſse but by gods aſſssiſſsstance
will vundauntedly proceede for god is able to reconcile all our
diferences

SrSir I humbly intreate you to ſsend mee a ſsmall feather
white and one tip of black by one Gregory Kent knowne
vunto mr Molloyne and beinge neare him he will be with mee
by Saturday at night I ſshall be very ijoyfull at the last
to heare of the welfare of you all thus coinge you
into the custody of the most heigh for present I
rest

postscript.p:
The bearer stayed the writinge therof which is the cause
my rustick ſscriblinge and inditinge

div1.p:
To his much Honored ffFrend
MrMaster George Willingham
Marchant at the
Golden Anchor
Swethins Lane

p.seg:
accordinge to custome I preſsent you with our pticularparticular
circumstances my last vunto you of this nature was SeptSeptember the 2d beinge Saturday
Sabath day septseptember the 3d wee peacably inijoyed

Munday morninge I was informed
by a cuntrey man of a baſse preist 6 miles diſstant which had ſset out horſse
for the commiſſssion of aray and had armes in his houſse and I immediatley got
20 muſsketteers and marched out to ſsearch the houſse the cuntrey man I clothed
with a ſsoildiers red coate gauve him armes and made him my guide but hauvinge
marched 2 miles certaine gentlemen of the cuntrey in formed mee that
IJustice Edmonds a man of good conuverſsation but ſsince I heare of the Aray was plundered by the baſse blewcoats
of colonell Cholmleys regiment and bereauved of his very beeds whervupon
I immediately devided my men into 3 ſsquadrons ſsurrounded them and forced
them to bringe ther pillage vupon their owne backs vunto the houſse againe for
which ſseruvice I was welcommed with the best varieties in the houſse and had
giuven me a ſscarlet Coate lined with pluſsh and ſseuverall exelent bookes in folio
of my owne chuſsinge but returninge a troope of horſse belonginge vunto Colonell
ffFoynes met mee pillaged mee of all and robbed mee of my very ſsword for which
cauſse I told them I would ether have my ſsword or dye in the feild commaunded
my men to charge with bullet and by ſsquadrons deuviſsions to fier vupon them which made
them with ſshame returne mee my ſsword and it beinge towards night I returned
to northampton threatninge revenge vupon the baſse troopers this night and
the day followinge our company by lot watched the ſsouth gate where I ſsearched
euvery horſsman of that troope to the ſskin tooke from them a fat buck a
veniſson pasty ready baked but lost my owne goods

wenſsday morninge wee
had tidings that prince Robert that diabolicall cauvalere had ſsurrounded Lester
and demaunded two thouſsand pounds or elſse threatned to plunder the towne
whervupon our ſsoildiers were euven madde to be at them but wanted commiſſssion
all the veniſson belonginge to malignants in the Cuntrey are destroyed

Thurſsday
our ſsoildiers marched in to the feild to exerciſse and there declared their baſse
ends ſspecified in a former letter compoſsed in hast and intended to be ſsent by
Leiftenant wade but he could not stay the wrightinge of it this day most
of the ministers nominated in your letter came unto vus

ffFryday morninge worthy
MrMaster obediah Sedgwich gauve us a worthy ſsermon and my company in pticularparticular
marched to heare him in ranke and file MrMaster John Sedgwich was appointed to preach
in the after noone but we had newes that prince Robert had plundered
Harbrough and fired ſsome adijacent townes and our Regimente were immediatly
drawne into the feild but beinge in formed of ther ffFlyinge away wee
returned

Saturday morninge MrMaster John Sedgwich gauve vus a famous ſsermon
after noone our regiments marched forth to meete his Exelency
who was in greate state welcommed into the towne and the watch
word this night was welcome this night and the day followinge our
company watched the northgate

Sabbath Day morninge MrMaster Marſshall
that worthy champion of Christ preacedpreached vunto vus after noone MrMaster Aſsh
by relation but as yet I hauve not ſseene him theſse with ther ſsermons
hauve already ſsubdued and ſsatisfied more malignante ſspirits amongst vus
then 1000 armed men could hauve done so that wee hauve greate hopes
of a bleſſssed vunion

Munday morninge I receiuved youyour letter dated
SeptSeptember the 8th with my Miſstriſses ſscarfe and MrMaster Molloynes hatband for
both which came very ſseaſsonably for I had gathered a little money together
and had this day made me a ſsoildiers ſsute for winter edged with gold and
ſsiluver lace theſse gifts I am vunworthy of I have nothinge to
tender you for them but humble and harty thankes I will weare them
for your ſsakes and I hope I ſshall neiuver staine them but in the
blod of a Cauvalleere Your letter beinge a pitthy ſsollid breife and
reall relation I preſsented to my Captaine and all the Captaines
of our regiment together at dinner with mrmaster Obbediah Sedgwich
who reijoysed at the newes and gauve me much thankes my Captaine
greetes you with his best reſspects

Tueſsday this day his Exelency
intends to view our forces wenſsday wee expect the Celebration
of a fast Thurſsday we expect to march with all our forces
Towards Lester and I doubt not but we ſshall ſscowre
the Cauvallers your man Dauvy remembers his ſseruvice vunto you and give
humble thankes for your kind remembrance of him I hauve not
any other thinge for the preſsent to acquaint you with Therfore
with my hublehumble ſseruvice to your ſselfe my Miſstris MrMaster Molloyne and
his wife with and vunto all yours and their Children and my louve to
the ſseruvants of both houſses I conclude vuntill Death remaingeremaininge

closer.salute:
your humble thankefull and deeply ingaged
ſseuvantservant at commaund

postscript.p:
Every wenſsday you may find a post that
ſseruveth our army at the Saracens
head in Carter lane his name is
Thomas weeden who is with vus
once a weeke constantly

To the worthy and his much
Honored ffFrend MrMaster George
Willingham Marchant
at the golden Anchor
in Swethins Lane
these preſsent

p.seg:
ſseptember the 13th was my last vunto you this euven wee had tidings that Killingworth
Castle in warwick ſshire 6 miles from Couventry was taken with store of ammunition and money
and ſsome priſsoners ther number vuncertaine the rest fled and the Cuntrey psuedperſsued them
and wanted but the aſſssistance of Couventry to destoydestroy them all

wenſsday ſsepſseptember the 14th our
forces bothe foote and horſse marched into the feild and the Lord generall veiwed vus both
both front reare and ffFlancks where the Drumms beatinge and the Trumpets ſsounding
made a harmony delectable to our frends but terrible to our enemies this euven
contrary to expectation our regiment marched 5 miles north east vunto
Spratton where wee and as many as could bilited in the towne the rest quartered
the cuntrey

Thurſsday our regiment met againe where thoſse famous lawes
for our army were read and expounded this day wee received and accepted
ſsargeant maijor Neale

ffFryday our regiment were commaunded to meete
here againe to be mustered where we exerciſsed in the feild the whole
day and the muster master came not wherat we were all much diſspleaſsed
this night our company by lot watched the towne this e

ſsaturday our
regiment met againe and weere mustered. this euven Captaine ffFrancis
returninge from London informed mee of the corragiouſsneſſsse and constancy
of the City of london and alſso of ther constant ſsupplyes of money and
plate and alſso told me that the whole City were now either reall or
constrained roundheads

Sabbath day wee peacably inijoyed with MrMaster Obbediah
Sedgwick who gauve us two heavenly ſsermons

Munday morninge our
regiment began to march towards warwick Shire and paſſssed through
west haddon Creeke and hill Morton where wee had a ſsuply of drinke
which upon a march is very rare and extreordinary welcome and at the
end of ten miles wee came to Rugby in warwick ſshire where we had
good quarter at this towne MrMaster Norton formerly preached this towne
alſso was lately diſsarmed by the Cauvallers on the ſsabbath day the
inhabitants beinge at Church

Tueſsday morninge our Regiment
marched 2 miles vunto Dunſsmore heath where the Lord Generall
and his Regiment met vus as alſso the Lord of Stanford Colonell
Cholmley and Colonell Hampden with many troopes of horſse and
18 feild peeces where we kept our randevoes vuntill euven where wee
had tidings that all the malignants in worſseſster Shire were with the
Cauvalleers were got into worſsester and fortified themſseluves whervupon
wee marched 6 miles vunto baggington within two miles of Couventry this night
the rest of our regiments quartered about the cuntrey

Thursday Wenſsday morninge
wee marched towards warwick leauvinge Killingworth Castle vupon the
right and after wee had marched 6 miles our forces met againe and quarted
before warwick vuntill 40 peeces of Ordinance with other carriadges paſſssed
by in which time I veiwed the antiquities about one mile on this side warwick
as SrSir Guyes cauve his Chappell and his picture in it his stables all hewed out
of the maine Rock as also his garden and 2 ſspringinge wels wherat he drank
as is reported from hence our regiment marched through warwick in
ſsuch hast that I could not veiw the towne but had only a ſsight of
the Castle which is very stronge built vupon a mighty rock wherof ther
are store in this Cuntrey this night we marched 2 miles further vunto
Burford where our quarter was as constantly ſsince his exelencyes comminge
it is very poore for many of our ſsoilders can get nether beads bread nor water
which makes them grow very stronge for backbiters hauve bin ſseene to march vupon
ſsome of them ſsixe on brest and eight deepe at their open order and I feare I
ſshall be in the ſsame condition eare longe for wee can get no carriadge for officers
so that my trunck and all neſſsseſſssaries therin are left at Couventry and indeede
our regiment is more ſslighted then any other which is cheifly occaſsioned as I
conceiuve partly by the falſse informations of leiftenant Colonell Briddeman
and our late Sargeant major Generall Ballard prophane wretches but cheifly
for want of our Colonell who ſshould be one of the counſsell of Warre at which
counſsell we have none to pleade for vus or remouve false aſsperſsions cast vupon
vus in so much that I hauve heard heard ſsome of our captaines repent their
comminge forth and all for want of a Colonell

Thurſsday morninge we marched
in the front 4 miles towards worceſster where wee met one ridinge post
from worceter informinge vus that our troopes and the Cauvallers were ther in fight
but it was falſse only to hast the captaines from Warwick vupon this report
our whole regiment ran ſshoutinge for 2 miles together and cryinge to worcester
to worcester and deſsired to march all night but after we had marched 2 miles
further we were commaunded to stand vuntill our forces paſſssed by and then
marched 2 miles further vunto Aſſssincantlo where wee could get no quarter
neither bread nor drinke by reaſson of the Lord Comptons late beinge there

ffFryday we marched 4 miles vunto Oster where our forces met and from thence
8 miles and incamped 4 miles on this ſside worſseſster but our ſsoildiers cryed
out for one hower together to goe forward to ſset vupon the enemy but could get
no commiſſssion this day we had such fowle wether that before I had marched
one mile I was weet to the ſskinne this day our horſse forces namely SrSir william
belfore Colonell Sands Colonell vines Colonell Clarke Maijor Duglas kept all the paſſssages
ouver Seuverne and by that meanes kept in the Cauvalleres who often aſſssayed to fly
but were prevented repelled theſse Commaunders ſsent to his Exelency for 3 feild peeces
and offered with them to keepe them in on that ſside vuntill wee had ſsurrounded
them but they were denied this day towards euven prince Robert entered the
City at a bye paſſssage with eighteene troopes of horſse most of the City cryinge
welcome welcome but principaley the Maior who deſsired to entertaine him but hee
anſswered god damne him he would not stay but would goe waſsh his hands in the
blod of the roundheads and immediately ſset ſsome to lye in ambuſsh and with
the rest ſsallyed out vupon the our forces and immediatly Colonell Fines Sands came
on brauvely euvene vunto the brest of their cheife commaunder and diſscharged
the rest vundauntedly followed but ther forces immediatly fled and ours followed
them and by the ambuſshment were beſset before and behind ſso that the battle
was very hot and many fell on both ſsides ſsome of our cheife commaunders
as Colonell Sands and Duglas was wounded but none ſslaine the and are ſsince both dead the cheife amongst
the Cauvalleeres were Prince Robert who I heare was wounded the Lord
Crauven and the Lord of Northhampton our wounded men they brought into the
City and stripped stabbed and ſslaſſssed ther dead bodies in a most barbarous manner
and imbrued their hands in their blode they also at ther returne met a yonge
gentlemen a parlaiment man as I am informed his name I cannot learne and
stabbed him on horſse back with many wounds and trampled vupon him and alſso most
maliciouſsly ſshot his horſse this euven our Generalls trope of gentlemen goinge to
quarter themſseluves about the cuntrey were betrayed and beſset by the enemy and
ouvermuch timerous immediately fled so confuſsedly that some brake their horſses necks
others their owne ſsome were taken others ſslaine and ſscarce halfe of them eſſssaped
which is ſsuch a blot vupon them as nothinge but ſsome deſsperate exploit will wipe of
hearinge this newes wee immediately cryed out to march vunto them and forwith drew
out a forlorne hope ſsome out of euvery company and ſsent them before intendinge to
march after them but about eleuven of the clock the enemies fled and our hope
returned here we aboade all night where we had ſsmall comfort for the it rained
hard our foode was fruite for thoſse that could get it our drinke water and beds the
earth our canopy the clouds but we pulled vup the hedges pales and gates and made
good fiers his exelency promiſsinge vus that if the cuntrey releiuved vus not the day
followinge he would fier ther townes thus we continued ſsinginge of pſsalmes vuntill
the morninge

Saturday morninge we marched vunto worſseſster our regiment in
the reare of the waggons the raine continuinge the whole day and the way
so baſse that we went vup to the ancles in thick clay and about 4 of the clock
after noone entred the city where we found where we found 28 dead men
which we buried ſsome of them Cauvallers and theſse were all that we can find
ſslaine on our ſside this euven by lot our company watched one of the gates and
alſso the day folloinge vuntill euven this euven his exelencyes guard entred the
maiors houſse and toke him priſsoner who is now more guarded then regarded

Sabbath day morninge our ſsoildiers entered a vault of the collidge where his
exelency was to heare a ſsermon and found eleuven barrels of gunpowder and a
pot of bullets this day MrMaster marſshall Sedgwich &cet cetera preached about the City but
I beinge vupon the court of guard could not heare them this euven his exelency
proclaimed that no ſsoildier ſshuld plunder either church or priuvate howſse vupon
paine of death

wee ſshortly expect a pitcht battell which if the Cauvallers
will but stand will be very hot for we are all much inraged against
them for their babariſsmesbarbarismes and ſshall ſshew them little mercy but I want time
to in large my ſselfe to conclude I humbly intreate you to preſsent my humble
ſseuviceservice to my MrsMistress as aſſssoalso MrMaster Edgertons our quartermaster and mine to MrMaster Molloyne
and his wife my ſseruvice alſso to MrMastery Hunt MrMaster Priaux MrMaster Simpſson and his
wife MrMaster Hawkins MrMaster Starkey &and I humbly in treate let me heare
from you of your welfare My Mistris and your family SrSir it is extreame
hast that makes me compoſse so confuſsedly and therfore with my ſseruvceservice
To MrMasterMrsMistress Elizabeth Anna John and little Sammuell and my louve to all my
fellow ſseruvants I rest yours in all good ſseruvices vuntill death

postscript.p:
My Captaine preſsents you with
his best reſspects and drinkes
to you euvery day we ſsit at table
together I hauve receiuved your
feather for which I giuve you
humble thankes

div1.p:
To the worthy and his much
Honored ffFrend MrMaster George
Willingham Marchant
at the golden Anchor
in StSaint Swethins Lane
These preſsent

opener.salute: My much honored MrMaster I humbly greete you

p.seg:
my last vunto you was SeptSeptember the 26th in which
there were ſsome errors occaſsioned partly by my ouverhastineſſsse in wrightinge for the bearer
promiſsed mee to deliuver it on wenſsday septseptember the 28th partly by the various relations
diſsperſsed but cheifly by reaſson I was vupon the guard and vupon paine of death durst
not stir from it to ſsesee or heare any occurrences but I had as good intelligence as the
Citty then afforded for the trewth of thinges was not then knowne the errors are theſse
ffFirst I wrote that the Earle of North hampton and the Lord Crauven were with the
Prince but they were not but vupon ſsuffitient information they were these Prince Robert Duke
Mawrice the Lord Digby Commiſſssary Wilmot SrSir Lewes Diuves SrSir William Ruſſssell
and Eſsquire Hastings a ſsecond was that most of the Curoſseers his Exelencies
trope were cut of but they are ſsince returned and but few lost but doe still beare
The aſsperſsion of cowards the third was that Colonell ſsands was dead but both he
and captaine Sands though both wounded yet are still liuvinge but that I may not trouble
you with common relations which commonly are fictions I hauve conferred with commaunders
the best intelligencers and hauve aſſssoalso veiwed the place where the battaile was fought but
breifly Worceſsterſshire is a pleaſsant fruitfull and rich Cuntrey aboundinge in corne
woods pastures hils and valleyes euvery hedge and heigh way beſset with fruite
but eſspecally with peares wherof they make that pleaſsant drinke called Perry
which they ſsell for a penny a quart though better then euver you tasted at
London Touchinge the City it is more Large then any I hauve ſseene ſsince I left
London and Like London it abounds in outwarde thinges of all kinds but for want
of the word the people perriſsh it is pleaſsantly ſseated exceedinge populous and
doubtleſse very rich it is scituate on the east banke of that famous Riuver
Seuverine the wals in the forme of a triangle the gates ſseauven the Bulwarkes
fiuve but much decayed no Castle, only a mount of earth in this Citty there is
a very stately Cathedrall called StSaint Maries in which there are many stately monuments
but amongst the rest in the middle of the quire is the monument of Kinge
John all of white marble with his picture theron to the life on the South ſside
Kinge Arthurs Tombe of Jette but no picture theron this Citty hath alſso a
stronge stone Bridge ouver ſseuverne conſsiſstinge of ſsixe arches with a gate
on the middle of the bridge as stronge as that on London Bridge with a pcullisporcullis
fiuve miles upon the Left of this is Maluvern hills which for height and
length and breadth doe many degres exceede all that euver I ſsee
I nominate them becauſse they are famous for on the top of them there is a
very brauve chaſse for many miles together a large ditch and ſsprings
alſso all on the very top betweene theſse hils and the riuver was the late
ſskermish about one mile from the City which was on this manner

Our troopes
on that ſside were deuvided to keepe the ſseuverall paſſssages and Colonell
Sands Colonell vines and sargeant Maijor Duglas with their Troopes were
set to keepe this paſſssage which was at the end of a narrow lane
which the treacherous inhabitants neare them diſscouvered to the Prince
and he forwith ſset ſsome troopes to lye in ambuſsh who brake downe a
hedge and lay in a feild on the right of them the treacherous citizens attendinge
them in multituds with muskets who lay on each ſside the hedge this done
the prince with other forces went to meete them but first ſsent a false alaram
informinge them that the Cauvaleers weere all fled and had left the City and alſso
that his exelency was come euven to the gates and immediately theſse 3 troopes
poasted away to meete his Exelency for SrSir william Belfore Colonell Clarke and
Our other commaunders heard not of it But hastinge downe A narrow lane
the prince met them Colonell Sands beinge in the front the Prince aſsked him
whom he was for, he anſswared for Kinge and Parlaiment he replyed not for
the kinge alone he anſswared no then ſsaid the Prince for the Kinge hauve
at you the Colonell anſswared for the Parlaiment hauve at you adand ſso
they diſscargeddischarged each at other the rest followed them and preſsently thoſse
in ambuſsh fired vupon them as alſso the muſsqetteers behind the hedges the
horſsemen charged not the ſsecond time but immediatly fell to their ſswords
ſso that for the ſspace of almost an hower the ſskermiſsh was excedinge hot
this relation I had from an gentleman that was in the front of the battell
and was wounded in with the ſsword and bullets in ſseuven ſseuverall places was
stripped naked and yet liuveth he affirmeth that though there were
ten for one yet there were more ſslaine and wounded of them then
of us and I ſspake with one that heard the Prince at his returne
ſsay that our men fought more like Lions then men our wounded
commaunders he brought into the City and gauve commaund that
that they ſshould be carefully looked vunto and with all ſspeed gathered
his forces together and fled leauvinge all their reconings to pay in ſsome
places 20 pounds in others ten in ſsome more ſsome leſſsse pretendinge and
alſso promiſsinge to returne ſsince their departure we heare that the
Prince is wounded but it is certaine Duke Mawrice is mortally wounded
they report vunto the Kinge that they have ſslaine eight hundred of
our men when there were but 28 ſslaine in all and ſsome of them were
Cauvalleeres of this I am certaine for I told all their grauves and
ſsearched the register of StSaint Jones parrish where they were all buried
they boast wonderfully and ſsweare most helliſshly that the next time
they meete vus they will make but a mouthfull of vus but I am
pſswadedperſswaded the Lord hath giuven them this ſsmall victory that they
may in the day of battell come on more preſsumptuouſsly to ther owne
destruction in which battell though I and many thouſsands more may bee
cut of yet I am confident the Lord of hoasts will in the end
triumph gloriouſsly ouver theſse horſses and all their Curſsed riders
They left at their flight in the City some horſses Truncks and other
thinges all which his exelency hath ſseazed on

Colonell Eſſssex is
made gouvernor of this City and his regiment ſshall be gariſsons here
SrSir Our army did little thinke euver to hauve seene Worcester but the
prouvidence of god hath brought vus heither and had it not the City
is ſso vile and the cuntrey ſso baſse ſso papisticall and Atheisticall
and Abominable that it reſsembles ſsodom and is the very Embleme of
Gomorah and doubtleſſsse it would hauve bin worſse then either Algiers
or Malta a very den of theeuves and a receptacle and refuge for all
the helhounds in the Cuntrey I ſshould hauve ſsaid in the land but wee hauve
handſsomley handled ſsome of them and doe cull out the rest as fast as wee
can who verbally cry pecauvi but cordeally itterum faciam and indeed
they doe as they are taught by DrDoctor Prediux late madde Byshop and
other popiſsh preists who are all run away.

to conclude Munday SeptSeptember 26th
one of Prince Roberts Trumpeters camescame to our gates and ſsounded a
point of warre who was preſsently taken and led blind fold through the
City vunto his Exelency This night Sargeant Maijor Duglas was nobly
buried

Tueſsday our ſsoildiers by commiſſssion from his exelency marched 7
miles vunto SrSir William Ruſſssels houſse and pillaged it vunto the bare
walls

Wenſsday wee fasted and MrMaster Obbediah Sedgwich preached vunto vus
whom the lord extreordineryly aſſssisted ſso that his doctrine wrought
wonderfully vupon many of vus and doubtleſſsse hath fitted many of vus for
death which wee all ſshortly expect

Thurſsday his Exelency proclaimed
that whoſsoeuver had any goods of the Cauvalleres in custody ſshould
forthwith ſsurrender them this day I mett with your ſseuvantservant Dauvy who
is in good health with his horſse he was on the west of Seuverne neare
the battell but vuntill it was ended heard not of it wee ijoyntly preſsent
you and my MrsMistress with our humble ſseruvice as alſso MrMaster Willingham your
Brother with his family MrMaster Chappels man and I doe preſsent our ſseruvice to
MrMaster Chappell and his wife MrMaster ffFelton and his wife and deſsire to heare
of their welfare

ffFryday morninge our drumms beate for our
Regiment to march away but wheither I know not wee ſshould bee
very glad to ſsee our Colonell SrSir I humbly intreate to excuſse my
late errors and to accept theſse my pore indeauvors beinge the last
I ſsuppoſse that euver I ſshall preſsent vunto you thus with my
dearest louve to all your children and my fellow ſseruvants wheither
with you and or from you beinge to march away in hast I must conclude

closer.salute: your everlouvinge humble thankfull and auntient ſseruvant

div1.p:
To the worthy and his much
Honored ffFrend MrMaster George
Willingham at the
Golden Anchor in
Sweethins Lane
London

p.seg:
ffFryday SeptSeptember the 30th was my last vunto you. this day a company of knights gentle
men and yeomen, of the County of Hereford, came to his Exelency, petioners for strength
to be ſsent ſspedily to Hereford. and forthwith wee were commaunded to draw out 15 men
out of euvery company in our Regiments, in all about 900, with 3 troopes of horſse and
2 peeces of Ordinance. with which we marched (a forlorne hope) towards Hereford.
our leaders were The Earle of Stanfords Leiftenant Colonell, Sargeant maijor Barrif, and Captain
Ingliſsby, of Colonell Hampdens ReRegiment, Captaine IJones of Cholmleys ReRegiment, Captaine Ward of Stanfords,
Captaine Pouvy of Hollis his regiment. beſsides Leiftenants and Sargeants. Our ministers
MrMaster John sedgwick, and MrMaster Kemme. after wee had marched 10 miles wee came to Bromyard,
the wether wet, and they way very fowle, here we got a little refreſshment and from hence marched
10 miles further to Hereford. but very late before wee got thither. and by reaſson of the raine and
ſsnow and extreamity of could one of our ſsoildiers died by the way. and it is wonderfull wee did
not all periſsh, for the cowardly Cauvalleers were within four miles of vus. in this poore condition
comminge to Hereford the gates were ſshut against vus, and for two howers we stood in dirt
and water, up to the midde legges for the City were all malignants, ſsauve three which were
roundheads. and the marqueſſsse of Harford had ſsent them word the day before, that they ſshould
in no wiſse let vus in. or if they did we would plunder their houſses, murder ther children,
burne their Bibles, and vutterly ruinate all. and promiſsed he would releive them himſselfe,
with all ſspeede for which cause the Citizens were reſsoluved to oppoſse vus vunto the death, and
hauvinge in the City three peeces of ordinance, charged them with nayles stones &cet cetera , and placed
them against vus, and wee against them, reſsoluvinge either to enter the City, or dye before it.
but the roundheads in the City, one of them an Alderman, Surnamed Lane: pſswadedperſswaded the
ſsilly maior, (for ſso hee is indeede) that his Exelency and all his forces weere at hand. whervupon
he opened vunto vus, and we entred the City at Bysters gate but. found the Dores ſshut, many
of the people with their children fled, and had enoffe to doe to get a little quarter but the
poore maior (ſseinge he was so handſsomly Cozoned) was not a little angry. for Harford with his
forces, which ffFled from Sherbon, promiſsed to viſsit them the day followinge. this night
though weet and weary, wee were faine to guard the City. this day our generall proclaimed,
that all delinquents that in ten daies would returne, and ijoyne with the parlaiment, ſshould
fauvorably, but conditionally, be excepted. exceptinge ſsuch as are members of the houſse,
which must ſsubmit to the ſsenſsure therof. But theſse by name are pticularlyparticularly excepted
The Earle of Bristo, the Earle of Cumberland, the earle of Newcastle, the Earle Riuvers,
secretary Nicolas, MrMaster Endymeon Porter, MrMaster Edward hide, The Duke of Richmond, the
Earle of Carnaruvan, the Lord viſscount Newwarke, The Lord viſscount ffFauckland,
his maijesties secretary in ſspetiall. This night thought weet and weary we were faine to guard
the City

Saturday our Squadron watcedwatched at StSaint Owens gate, which day I tooke an
opportunity to veiw the City, which is well ſscituate, and ſseated upon the riuver Y.
inuvironed with a stronge wall, better then any I hauve ſseene before, with 5 gates and
a stronge stone bridge of ſsixe arches, ouver the riuver, ſsurpaſſssinge worſseſster. in this
City there is the statlyest market place in the Kingdome. built with Cullumnes, after
the maner of the Exchange. the Minster euvery way exceedinge that at worcester.
but the City in Circuit not ſso large. the inhabitants are totally ignorant in the waies
of god and much addicted to drunkenneſſsse, and other vices, but principally vunto
ſswearinge ſso that the children that hauve ſscarce learned to ſspeake, doe vuniverſsally
ſsweare stoutly. many here ſspeake welsh.

this day our companies exerciſsinge in the
feilds at worſseſſsster, one of The Lord Generals soildiers ſshot at randum, and with
a brace of bullets, ſshot one of his fellow ſsoildiers through the head, who
immediatly dyed,

Sabbath day, about the time of morninge prayer, we went to the Minster, where
the pipes played, and the puppets ſsange ſso ſsweetely, that ſsome of our ſsoildiers
could not forbeare dauncinge, in the holy quire: wherat the Baallists were ſsore diſsplesd
the Antheam ended they fell to prayer, and prayed deuvoutly, for the Kinge, the Biſshops &cet cetera
and one of our ſsoildiers with a loud voice ſsaide, what neiuver a bit for the Parlaimen
which offended them much more. not ſsatiſsfied with this humane ſseruvice, we went to
deuvine, and paſſssinge by found ſshops open, and men at worke. to whom wee gauve ſsome
plaine dehortations, and went to heare MrMaster Sedgwick, who gauve us two famous
ſsermons: which much affected the poore inhabitants, who wonderinge ſsaid, they neiuver
heard the like before. and I beleeuve, them, the Lord moouve your harts to commiſserate
ther diſstreſſsses, and to ſsend them ſsome faithfull and painfull ministers, for the reuvennews
of the Collidge, will maintaine many of them. This euven the Earle of Stanford
(who is made gouvernor of the City Hereford) entred the City, with a Regiment of
foote, and ſsome troopes of horſse: and tooke vup the Biſshops Pallace, for his quarter. and is
resoluved, there to abide whervupon

On Munday morninge, we marched towards
Worcester, and at the end of ten miles came to Bromyard, where we quartered all
night, This day his Exelency proclaimed, that all ſsoildiers that would ſset to didginge
ſshould hauve tweluve pence the day, and enter into pay preſsently.

Tueſsday wee marched
to worcester, and weere received with much ijoy. for the Deſseigne was ſso
deſsperate, that our IJuditious frends, neiuver looked to see vus againe. I am in
good health, and by the goodneſſsse of god ſsupplyed with strenghstrength, beyond expectation.

Wenſsday morninge, I went to veiw the ſsoildiers workes, who hauve pourtraed out
the ſseuverall formes of their Scaunces, halfe moones, Redouts, &cet cetera beginninge at
Seuverne on one ſside, of the City, and goe round the City vunto Seuverne againe.
it will be finished with all conuvenient ſspeede. for as wee intrench here ſso
alſso doth Prince Robber, at Bridge norton, tweluve miles of. and we heare at
Beaudle alſso, from whence commeth the coales, that ſsupply Our City. but we hauve
ſsent out ſsome forces to expell them thence. this day after noone, at the request
of my Captaine and other commaunders: I againe rode with them vunto Maluverne
hils, forementioned, leauvinge our horſses in the towne, after much toyle we aſſsscended
the hills, which indeede are a very Curious proſspecte for the day beinge cleare,
wee could see neare thirty miles round, all the valley betweene vus and woster,
though fiuve miles broad, and many miles longe, (incloſsed with hedges) ſsemed vunto
vus, but as a garden with a few knots in it, (though indeede they are very large
pastures) at the bottome of theſse hils is Maluverne Church, the statlyest
parriſsh Church in England. adorned with varieties of rarities, which I
want time to expreſſsse.

Thurſsday wee exerciſsed our ſsoildiers in the feilds, this day
The Lord of Coventry came in to vus. and this euven we expected 3 lords more with a
Meſſssage from his maijesty,

ffFryday a pare of gallowes were ſset up: in the market place,
for the villan that betrayed our troopes, auvoide

I
hauve breifly ſsent you euvery dayes, paſſssage ſsince I left London which I hope you
hauve receiuved. I earnestly deſsire to heare of the welfare of you, my MrsMistress, and
Your whole family, by this bearer, Thomas Weeden, who weekely viſsits our army, and
is faith full. he lodgeth at the Saracens head, in Carter lane. SrSir I greete you and
my MrsMistress with my most humble ſseruvice, as alſso MrMaster Molloyne and his Wife, vunto whom
I am much ingaged principally for his deuvine exortation, to reade thoſse 2 chapters
which I and my company hauve often done, they beinge very ptinentpertinent to the deſseigne
in hand. I pray excuse my longe ſsilence towards him and assure him that I will pticularlyparticularly preſsent
him, with the next remarkeable paſſssage. I would hauve done it before this time,
but your Athenians catch it from vus, and carry it post vunto you, (though for the most
more then is true) that before we can get conuveyance, it is turned into antiquity
thus with my louve and ſseruvice to MrsMistress Elizabeth, Anna, John, and little Sammuell, and my
louve to all my fellow ſseruvants, of both ſsexes, for the preſsent I rest, but not ſseaſse
to remaine vuntill death:

closer.salute: Your auntient, humble, and affectionate ſseruvant,
